purpose: Map all 27 existing findings to implemented changes, executed checks and explicit remaining acceptance work. This report consolidates existing evidence; it provides no blanket security, performance or release certification.

status_definitions.implemented_and_verified: The stated code/documentation defect has an implemented repair and relevant executed checks. This is bounded to cited evidence; it is not final CI, release, formal-security or all-platform certification.
status_definitions.implemented_pending_qualification: Implementation and focused verification exist, but a material acceptance step such as hosted, platform, artifact, realistic-workload or controlled-run qualification remains pending.
status_definitions.partially_remediated: A substantive portion is repaired, while a material implementation/architecture/advisory or production-integration gap remains. Do not mark closed.
status_definitions.prepared_not_applied: A concrete change payload and validation exist, but the external control has not been applied or read back. Do not describe it as enforced.

findings.title: Bounded payload buffering does not bound dense-record metadata memory

changes.summary: Online record visitors absorb dense boundaries during traversal and scan accepted segments immediately, removing production candidate/accepted-cut/segment materialization.

The dense header window is allocated once at its bound (left to grow, it doubled and on macOS briefly held two copies: 48.7 MiB); the qualification models a fixed workspace per kind of log and measures random, non-periodic logs.

The dense walk's read-ahead and hashing batch were then cut from 16 MiB and 8 MiB to 64 KiB, so a dense log needs no more workspace than a sparse one (about 2.4 MiB), and the original limit on the dense-minus-sparse difference is enforced again. Each run now also reports scan speed relative to the plain log.

The per-record memory check was sitting at its limit and failed once on hosted Linux with unchanged scanner code. Its model let the plain log fix the per-chunk cost, which three hosted reports show it cannot. The check now compares two dense logs of one size with different record sizes, so the chunk count is held nearly fixed; the limits are unchanged, and a pair that cannot tell is refused instead of passed. CI sizes moved from 256 and 1024 MiB to 192 and 768 MiB, clear of a measured step in peak memory at power-of-two chunk counts.

validation.summary: A two-million-record reader contract and 18 paired memory observations verify online behavior. At four million records, median native VmHWM decreased by 94.1 percent while exact output digests matched.

Hosted on c3cd967: scan memory qualification (ubuntu-latest); scan memory qualification (windows-latest); scan memory qualification (macos-latest) passed. Dense, sparse and plain logs of 256 MiB and 1 GiB on each platform: every workspace within its declared bound, per-record slope at most 0.05 bytes.

Hosted on 403c77f, Linux, Windows and macOS: the redesigned check passed on all three. Per-record memory read between -0.011 and +0.003 bytes per record against a limit of 0.05, resolving 0.004 to 0.024 where 0.125 is required; the dense and mid logs returned 12,327 to 12,492 chunks (10,572 to 10,694 for plain CDC). On Linux, where the previous model had read 0.0501, it read -0.0001. The whole run passed: 59 checks, none failed.

remaining: Hosted sizes stop at 1 GiB; larger logs were measured on one Windows workstation only.

The smaller buffers cost speed: about 15 to 30% on dense logs and up to a third on sparse ones (hosted runners and a 14-round workstation sweep agree on the direction; the workstation is too noisy to pick an optimum). A larger hashing batch with a small read-ahead should keep the memory limit and restore parallel hashing; that needs a quiet machine.
Returned output remains O(chunks), and the explicit offset-list APIs keep their O(records) result by design.

findings.title: New file APIs have no binding-level tests or in-repository runtime integration evidence
findings.acceptance: Exercise the installed Python wheel's new exports, error mappings, selected parameters, path handling, each format and the 256 MiB refusal/fallback contract. Add a bounded synthetic reader fixture to cross the real window without expensive disk tests, and randomize valid profiles/chunked reads for differential tests. Treat end-to-end product performance as unqualified until a real caller and benchmark are recorded.

changes.summary: Installed exports now have format/profile/path/error/window/limit tests. Separately accelerated the existing descriptor-bound production Gear CDC path without substituting the distinct pathname/format-aware Rust semantics.

Descriptor-bound scans (cdc_fd, format_aware_fd) read the caller's verified open file, so a pathname replaced after verification cannot change the boundaries; binding tests cover every export, error mapping and refused profile.

validation.summary: The 107 binding and export cases passed, including a real 32 MiB window crossing and 256 MiB refusal. Production Gear acceleration has exact-boundary evidence.
The format-aware file API has a production caller, and its suite passes on this branch's wheel.

remaining: No end-to-end benchmark with the real caller is recorded.
One Link's own transfer path stays on plain content-defined chunking on purpose: a deduplication experiment on its corpus did not favour format-aware cuts.

findings.title: cdc_file documentation still describes a 512 KiB buffer despite a 32 MiB window
findings.acceptance: Describe payload window, candidate metadata and output-vector growth separately rather than quoting a 512 KiB bound.

changes.summary: Corrected Rust and Python documentation and exported constants: the default payload window is 32 MiB, or four times the maximum chunk size when larger. Kernel workspace and output or metadata growth are described separately.

validation.summary: Runtime limit constants and window/refusal contracts are exercised by installed-wheel tests.

remaining: No constant-total-memory claim; output size and explicit all-offset APIs remain proportional to their result counts.

findings.title: Cross-platform determinism fixture does not yet pin exact boundary outputs
findings.acceptance: Pin a reviewed boundary/hash golden vector for representative profiles and execute it on x86_64/ARM64 and supported operating systems.

changes.summary: Pinned exact pre-change starts/ends/hashes and corpus hashes for random/zero/edited fixtures; serial/parallel/streamed kernels share reviewed golden outputs.

validation.summary: Frozen vectors passed in local Linux package tests. Existing all-targets/all-features OS/architecture workflow includes the integration fixture.

Initial hosted Linux x86_64/ARM64 and macOS native jobs passed. Windows exposed an LF-only parser. The repair passes against LF/CRLF while keeping all frozen golden outputs unchanged, and all six tests passed on actual Windows.

Hosted on c3cd967: cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-latest); cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-24.04-arm); cargo test (workspace) (windows-latest); cargo test (workspace) (macos-latest) passed. The pinned boundary and hash vectors, including the v2 format-aware vectors, run on x86_64 and ARM64 Linux, Windows and macOS.

remaining: Format-aware boundaries changed definition (version 2); stores that mix versions deduplicate only where the definitions agree.

findings.title: Shamir sharing forbade a zero top coefficient, which broke perfect secrecy
findings.acceptance: Every polynomial coefficient is uniform over GF(2^8); k-1 shares give no information about the secret.

changes.summary: The re-roll of the top coefficient is gone: with it, anyone holding k-1 shares could rule out one secret value per byte, and the loop branched on a secret. GF(256) inversion and division are branch-free.

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: constant-time dataflow audit (valgrind) passed. Exhaustive tests enumerate every (secret, coefficient) pair for k=2 and every pair of shares for k=3; reinserting the re-roll fails both.

findings.title: Secret-dependent branches and table lookups in onion, key-encapsulation and duress code
findings.acceptance: No branch or memory index depends on a secret outside a marked, reasoned verdict line.

changes.summary: Nine early-exit all-zero tests on shared secrets in the onion and obfuscation code are constant-time.
ml-kem 0.2.3 indexed a table by bits of the decrypted message during decapsulation; the upstream fix is backported into a vendored, provenance-checked copy.
The duress gate decided real, duress or rejected with measurably different timing; DuressGate::decide computes all three uniformly. Found by the statistical test on both hosts.
The QUIC certificate-fingerprint timing test compared with a function defined in the test; the production comparison now uses a constant-time primitive and is the thing audited.

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: constant-time dataflow audit (valgrind) passed.

remaining: See RLS-05 for what a Valgrind audit and a noisy-host statistical test do not prove.

findings.title: Chunk profiles FastCDC refuses aborted the process or looped without bound
findings.acceptance: Every scan entry point refuses an invalid profile with an error, and no input makes a walker overflow.

changes.summary: Parameter bounds come from the FastCDC constants; the parallel kernel returns NoProgress instead of looping (a 100-byte file had tried to allocate 27 GB); one checked walker per container format serves both the in-memory and the file path (a 16-byte MP4 had indexed past the end).

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-latest); cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-24.04-arm); cargo test (workspace) (windows-latest); cargo test (workspace) (macos-latest) passed.

findings.title: Format-aware chunking did not resynchronise on dense records
findings.acceptance: An insertion, deletion or edit changes chunk boundaries only near itself, whatever the record size.

changes.summary: Boundary definition version 2: dense candidates are thinned by a fingerprint and kept only at a strict local maximum, so an edit moves cuts only within a bounded distance. One record inserted into 64 MiB of 32-byte records re-sent 100% of the file before and 0.03 MiB after.

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-latest); cargo test (workspace) (ubuntu-24.04-arm); cargo test (workspace) (windows-latest); cargo test (workspace) (macos-latest) passed.

remaining: Peers on different boundary versions deduplicate each other only on sparse containers; FORMAT_AWARE_CHUNKING_VERSION is exported so a store can record which definition made a manifest.

findings.title: Setting or unsetting the passphrase variable replaced the key that protected an install's data
findings.acceptance: No start, export or recovery path can replace a data key that still protects rows or files; changing the protection is an explicit, crash-replayable migration.

changes.summary: Mint guards refuse at every place a data key is created; one registry lists every artifact a data key protects and proves which key opens it by trying; key-authority failures stop startup instead of degrading to a stateless daemon.
Identity rotation re-keys every key-protected state field in one transaction.

`one-link recovery set-passphrase` and `remove-passphrase` migrate an install between protections, replayable after a crash at any step; a passphrase-protected install started without its passphrase refuses to start and names both fixes; a wait on the key lock is logged, bounded on the event loop and cannot wait on itself.

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: full pytest suite / ubuntu-latest / py3.12; full pytest suite / windows-latest / py3.12 passed.

remaining: An install already split across two data keys now refuses to start with an explicit message; before, it kept writing under a key that did not protect its data.
After set-passphrase the old stored database key stays in the keychain; it opens nothing.

Four test daemons in a row on a hosted Windows runner stalled 26 to 30 s where the data key is acquired. The cause was not found. Two real lock defects on that path are fixed (366c047), the event-loop wait is capped at 2 s, and a slow step now logs where it is stuck.

findings.title: A resumed or retried transfer dropped the requested transport and undercounted itself
findings.acceptance: Resume keeps the transport the user asked for, and a transfer's ledger row describes the whole transfer.

changes.summary: Durable resume and manual retry rebuild send arguments through one function, so a transfer asked to use TCP no longer resumes as 'auto' and rides the relay.
The ledger row covers every attempt; resumed bytes are no longer booked as savings; the route snapshot states its unit.

validation.summary: Two of the three accounting claims the review raised were refuted or latent; the tests that settled each are kept.

remaining: The planner's estimate can show a few percent 'already known' on a send with no savings; not fixed here.

findings.title: No tag ruleset and no protected release environment
findings.acceptance: Release tags cannot be created, moved or deleted outside the release process, and signing waits for a protected environment.

changes.summary: Signing and publication name `environment: release`; the tag-ruleset and environment payloads are written out.

validation.summary: Read back: neither exists yet.

remaining: Applying either is a repository-owner decision; this review changed no repository setting.

findings.title: Required native gates could pass without running
findings.acceptance: A change that can affect native results always runs the native work, and a pull request cannot edit the policy that decides this.

changes.summary: The applicability policy is default-applicable (every path runs the work unless a reviewed rule says no job reads it) and both the applicability and the gate step run the base revision's copy of it. Secret-scan exceptions are anchored on content instead of commit ids, so a squash merge cannot turn the full-history scan red.

validation.summary: Hosted on c3cd967: native correctness applicability; native performance applicability; native shell applicability; Gitleaks full-history scan passed.

remaining: This pull request is the bootstrap case: the base revision has no policy yet, so the base-copy protection takes effect once it merges.
A pull request can still edit the workflow file itself; the settings that close that are in docs/RELEASE_PROTECTION.md.

findings.title: Ending an inbound call threw, skipping media teardown
findings.acceptance: Call teardown releases the microphone and camera whatever else fails.

changes.summary: The call driver referenced another closure's names and threw `state is not defined`; the handler swallowed it, so ringing UI and media teardown were skipped. Teardown now runs first. The same class of reference made the privacy panel's preset switch appear to work when it did nothing.

validation.summary: Four teardown cases fail on the previous revision; 34 cross-closure references are 0 and a gate fails on any new one.
Hosted on c3cd967: e2e (playwright) / ubuntu-latest; e2e (playwright) / windows-latest passed.

findings.title: A QUIC throughput regression was read as a pass
findings.acceptance: A regime the gate cannot see is measured and reported, not discarded.

changes.summary: The five-pair study's slower 16 KiB QUIC result was the process's first QUIC traffic, which the twenty-pair study's untimed warm-ups covered and threw away. An explicit ungated first-traffic probe now runs before any gated QUIC metric, and warm-up timings are kept.

validation.summary: Ruled out by analysis of both runs' artifacts: a code change in One Link's QUIC, metric order, a per-call fixed cost, and steady state (0.9942 [0.9867, 1.0017] over twenty pairs).

The new probe, paired over the twenty pairs of the hosted benchmark run at c7d57a1: median first traffic 4.56 ms on the base and 4.71 ms on the candidate; geometric-mean ratio 1.17 with a 95% interval of [0.96, 1.42]; the candidate slower in 14 of 20 pairs and with a slow tail (31 ms at worst, against 5 ms).

remaining: The first-traffic explanation survived the elimination and the probe points the same way, but the interval includes no difference: it is not established at twenty pairs. In the median the effect is under a fifth of a millisecond, once per process.

findings.title: Evidence and gates that could mislead
findings.acceptance: A committed ledger agrees with its report and with history, and a published report names no machine detail.

changes.summary: The ledger's counts must equal its findings, the report's table must state the same counts, and every cited commit and evidence id must exist.
The timing report wrote an absolute path and the names of unrelated processes on the measuring machine; both are gone by default, before any such report was committed.
The scan-memory gate reported O(records) memory for a scanner whose memory was flat; its model, its corpus and a real allocation overshoot behind the numbers were each corrected.

validation.summary: Each gate has tests that make it fail as well as pass.

remaining: Older tracked audit files in this public repository contain a local user-profile path; removing them from history is an owner decision.

findings.title: Every daemon restart invalidated every saved window sign-in
findings.acceptance: A browser session minted before a daemon restart authenticates after it, for any number of restarts, and re-opening a populated database changes no row.

changes.summary: The schema runner re-applies every migration step on every start. Step 28, which replaces each stored session bearer with its SHA-256 record key, is one-way, and a record key has the shape of a bearer, so each start hashed the stored keys again. In master since 2026-07-25. One-way steps are now listed and skipped once the database has reached their version; the stamp is written in the same transaction as the step.

A refused owner request now leaves one line saying where a credential was presented and whether it has the shape of a session bearer (never the credential). Its first use is what identified this defect.

The re-open test's helper guarded its folder row on a column the table does not have, so the check covered two tables while claiming more (found by the independent read). It now writes real rows to four tables with no guard that can skip them and asserts each is populated before comparing re-opens.

validation.summary: Measured on a real daemon before the fix: the window's bearer answered 200, then 401 after a restart on the same home and port, and the stored record key had changed. After: 200 both times, key unchanged. Seven state tests, five of which fail with the defect put back; one live test restarts a real daemon twice.

Hosted on 6eb2af7: 59 checks passed, none failed, 2 skipped. Both full suites, all eight live shards and both browser lanes passed, including the live test that restarts a real daemon twice. An independent adversarial read could not make the step apply twice: two processes opening at once, twenty crash points across steps 27 to 30, and every starting version from 1 to 30 all ended with the step applied once.

On the install where it was found, across the restart that rolled this fix (2026-11-26): the stored record keys of its four saved sign-ins were identical before and after. Under the old code every restart changed them.

remaining: Not covered: a binary older than step 28 writing into a database already past it leaves a row the step will not convert. That row cannot authenticate, so the browser signs in once more. Making the step idempotent needs a stored form that tells a record key from a bearer.
Rolled onto the install where it was found. The owner's second device still runs older code. Sign-ins invalidated before the roll cannot be restored.

findings.title: An owner window showed two status banners over each other and never recovered by itself
findings.acceptance: The window shows at most one status, in the layout flow; while its credential is not disproved it keeps retrying and resumes with nobody touching it; it calls itself signed out only after the daemon has refused the credential twice.

changes.summary: One service owns the window's link to the daemon and the one status line. The session banner was a second element fixed where the status line sits; recovery was attempted at most twice per page; the page said 'expired' when the daemon had merely not answered. The event socket counts as connected when the daemon greets it, not when it opens: the daemon accepts an unauthenticated socket and closes it with 4401.

validation.summary: 18 unit tests with a virtual clock, 30 of 30 planted defects caught. In a real browser against a real daemon: a window left open across a restart on the same port recovers untouched; with FLD-01 put back the same test fails with the window correctly signed out on one line. Signed-out, offline and narrow layouts are checked geometrically.

Hosted on 6eb2af7: 59 checks passed, none failed, 2 skipped. Both full suites, all eight live shards and both browser lanes passed; the three browser tests, including the real daemon restart, passed on hosted Linux and Windows.

On that install after the roll: the native window opened signed in on the fixed page with no browser fallback. The daemon's refusal note recorded the old window's two refused requests before that window was closed, and none afterwards.

remaining: What first answered 401 to the window on 2026-11-25 was not recorded anywhere; FLD-01 explains a 401 after the restart, and the daemon now records the next one.
The call backfill poll is not suspended during recovery, and the update, key-rotation and install banners are still fixed overlays at the top of the window.

The browser restart test failed once on hosted Linux for a reason in the test (a probe count over a fixed window). It was corrected to count from the injected 401; with recovery capped at two attempts it still fails.

findings.title: A file waiting for the owner's acceptance made the sender's later files fail
findings.acceptance: While an offer waits for the owner, a second send of that file, further files beyond the per-device limit, and the waiting session itself are all told to wait; none is refused for load and the waiting session is not closed at the ordinary idle limit.

changes.summary: A held offer keeps its blob entry and admission reservation, and the offer handler read that as a transfer in progress: a second send was refused as content in use by another delivery, a fourth file as over quota, and the receiver closed the waiting session at 120 seconds although the sender waits 300. Each now gets FILE_OFFER_HELD or the acceptance window. An acceptance that could not be delivered is inherited by the same file sent again.

An inherited acceptance now also requires the declared size the owner saw. Admission reserves the declared size and receives up to it before the content hash can be checked, so the same hash re-offered with a larger size would have been given storage the owner never agreed to (found by the independent read, before any release). A decline after an undeliverable acceptance is shown to leave nothing to inherit.

validation.summary: 21 unit tests, 8 planted wrong decisions each caught. Four tests between two real daemons with the real accept API, the first to accept a held offer end to end; with the three defects put back three of them fail, one with the incident's own error.

Hosted on 6eb2af7: 59 checks passed, none failed, 2 skipped. Both full suites, all eight live shards and both browser lanes passed, including the four two-daemon tests. The size check added afterwards has run on a workstation only.
Hosted on 9428729, which contains the size check: 59 checks passed, none failed, 2 skipped. Both full suites, all eight live shards and both browser lanes passed.

remaining: What keeps this pending: inheriting an undeliverable acceptance is unit-tested but not exercised between two real daemons, and the independent read of this change was by reading, not execution.

Read from the code, not measured: once the stall deadline parks an accepted offer whose sender never returned, a different delivery of the same file is refused as resume_owned_by_another_delivery, even when the parked copy holds no bytes. The inheritance above covers only the time before that.
A waiting sender is not told when the wait ends; it finds out on its next retry.
'Accept all from this device' is remembered only until the daemon restarts; whether it should persist is an owner decision.
If an inheriting delivery is then refused for another reason (disk space, say), the acceptance is not kept and the owner is asked again. Read from the code; not exercised.

findings.title: A daemon asked to stop kept running while any connection stayed open
findings.acceptance: A daemon that acknowledges a stop exits cleanly within seconds, whatever is connected to it: a message-tail subscriber, a quiet peer session, a command in progress or a held file offer.

changes.summary: Since Python 3.12 a closed asyncio server waits for every connection it accepted; the stop path was written for the earlier behaviour. A stop therefore waited for each peer session to go quiet for its idle limit and, indefinitely, for any message-tail subscriber. The daemon now registers what its two servers accept and ends those connections itself when it stops, whether the stop is requested or the serving task is interrupted.

After an independent review: a connection that is closing is not yet closed. One closed with bytes still unsent to a client that has stopped reading stays registered until its transport lets go, and the stop gives it the grace period and aborts it like any other; before, the stop skipped it and could wait on it for ever. Connections are also ended once in every case, which before Python 3.12 they were not when the servers had been closed before the stop looked.

validation.summary: Measured on scratch daemons, Python 3.12.13. Before: nothing connected, stopped in 1.8 s; a tail client attached or one quiet peer session, still running 45 s after acknowledging the stop. After: 0.2 to 1.5 s and exit code 0 in every case, including a held file offer. Eleven tests against real asyncio servers (14 of 14 planted defects caught) and three tests with real daemons, all three of which fail with the defect put back.

Hosted on 4621947: both full suites, all eight live shards (whose manifest includes the three real-daemon stop tests), both browser lanes and the four unit lanes passed. Four checks failed for reasons outside this finding: the scan-memory per-record model on Linux with its roll-up, and one inconclusive disk benchmark with its roll-up.

On the install (2026-11-26): the daemon running the old code, asked to stop with a message tail attached, was still running ten seconds later and exited within 0.2 s of the tail ending. The next start reported no unclean shutdown. The new daemon's own stop has not been exercised there.

Independent review (a reviewer that did not write it), by reading and three small experiments; it reached its limit before running either test file, a planted defect or a real daemon. It found no way to make the stop fail. It found a test helper that could not fail: a timeout was caught with the connection errors and counted as an ended connection, under eight assertions. Corrected, the eight still pass, and a test shows the helper saying no. It named the closing-connection case without being able to produce it on Windows; that is now tested with a scripted writer on every platform and with real sockets where bytes are left unsent. It asked what unanswering browser windows do to a stop: measured with two such event sockets on a real daemon, 1.3 s, now a real-daemon test. Six planted defects in the module and its helper are each caught.

remaining: An explicit stop now interrupts a transfer or a control command in progress instead of waiting for it, which is what it did before Python 3.12. The updater's own drain still refuses to begin while transfers are active.
The interrupt path (Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break) is covered against real asyncio servers but not by a real-daemon test.
On Python 3.11 a closed server does not wait, so only the 3.12 lanes can fail these tests.
Not examined, by the author or the reviewer: what a stop does to a handler caught in the middle of a durable change. The stores are closed one loop turn after the connections are ended, as before.
The real-socket test of a closing connection skips on Windows, where the platform accepted all 64 MiB at once; the scripted-writer tests run everywhere.
Hosted CI on the revision with these corrections.

findings.title: A file sender and its receiver could each wait for the other until the send was reported as paused
findings.acceptance: A file send never stops to wait for an acknowledgement the receiver is not going to send, with a receiver of this version or an earlier one; a receiver answers a sender of an earlier version that stops early; and a chunk the receiver refuses ends the send with the receiver's reason.

changes.summary: A sender tells the receiver how many chunks to acknowledge together, taken from its send window, and stopped whenever the window was full. A slow acknowledgement halves the window. Read between sending a chunk and deciding to stop, it left the sender waiting with fewer chunks outstanding than that chunk had announced, and the receiver holding all of them until more arrived. Neither had a timer shorter than the sender's 30-second limit. The sender now stops only when it has at least as many chunks outstanding as its last chunk announced, and otherwise sends one more; the receiver now answers a batch that has stayed short for a tenth of a second. Either change is sufficient alone, so a pair of mixed versions is covered in both directions. The defect dates from 2026-05-12 and is on the default branch.

An independent review refuted the first claim in one case: a receiver that refuses a chunk says so at once while it may hold the answers to the chunks before it, and the sender's reply wait dropped an answer to any chunk but the one it awaited before checking whether it was a refusal. The sender then waited out its deadline and reported a silent peer; with the new timer the held answers were also sent after the transfer had been abandoned. The sender now takes a refusal of any chunk it has outstanding as the refusal of the transfer, and a receiver that abandons a transfer drops what it held. The stall predates the first change; the late answer did not.

After a second independent review: the receiver's short-batch timer asks, when it fires, whether its file is still the one in progress, and drops what it held if not. Not every path that ends a transfer goes through the abort that the previous change taught to drop held answers; the reviewer counted eight refusal sites without it.

validation.summary: A search of every reachable state of the send loop against the receive rule, driven by the real window controller, over 288 configurations and transfers of up to 12 chunks: with the rule that shipped, 252 configurations can stall, the smallest after three chunks; with the sender's new rule alone, none; with the receiver's new rule alone, none. A first version of the sender's rule, which only booked batched acknowledgements earlier, was refuted by the same search (238 configurations still stalled) and discarded. With the receiver refusing each chunk in turn, every history ends with the sender told of the refusal, against a receiver of either version. 31 planted defects are each caught; the seven that remove a call from the daemon's send path are caught only by a check of the source text.

Measured between two freshly paired daemons on a workstation, a 64 MiB file each time: before, 4 of 134 sends stalled for 30 seconds and were reported as paused; after, 189 of 189 completed (126 on the committed code, 63 on an earlier arrangement of the same rule), with the median send time unchanged at 1.9 s. In one of 63 instrumented sends the sender's new rule was needed, six times; without it each was a stall.

Independent review of the first change (a reviewer that did not write it): refuted for a refused chunk, with a runnable two-chunk witness against the real receive handlers and the real reply wait; addressed as above. It confirmed by reading that the last chunk always announces a batch of one in both loops. It did not examine the ordering of the timer's frame against the handler's on one channel, the bound on sending past a full window, or the soundness of the search's pruning.

Second independent review, of the refused-chunk change: the sender's side confirmed by reading (the two send loops are alternatives, nothing recovers from the raise inside either, and a refusal of a pending chunk was already fatal before, by timeout; the offer and commit waits cannot be affected). The receiver's claim could not be decided and had static evidence against it, addressed as above. Its mutation runs showed that unwiring the refusal check, or the queues it reads, is caught only by the test that reads the source text: no test drives the daemon's reply wait with a refusal out of turn. 35 planted defects in this finding's rules are each caught.

remaining: Hosted CI on these revisions.

No test with real daemons fails deterministically without the first change: the stall needs a slow acknowledgement at one point in the transfer, and nothing in the product lets a test place it. The evidence with real daemons is the before-and-after count.

A sender that predates the second change still waits out its deadline when a chunk behind a held answer is refused, whatever the receiver runs. Answering what is held before every refusal would fix that for old senders and means touching about forty refusal sites; not done.
The reply wait's handling of a refusal is tested through the function it calls and a check of the source text, not by driving the daemon's send path; an independent review confirmed it by reading.

The window controller is told an acknowledgement's age when the send loop next needs room, not when the acknowledgement arrived, so chunks answered together look progressively slower and the window shrinks more often than the link warrants. Recorded, not changed: it affects speed, not completion.

The disabled QUIC chunk path derives its transfer session from the most recent inbound connection from the peer, which can be a route-verification probe. Read in the source, not tested; the path is off.

findings.title: A daemon that had rotated its identity froze the connection of a peer that called it
findings.acceptance: A daemon that owes a caller a rotation certificate delivers it and goes on answering that caller, and nothing outlives the connection.

changes.summary: After the CAPS exchange each daemon sends the other any rotation certificate it still owes, from inside its CAPS handler. On a ratcheted channel the side that accepted the connection cannot send until it has read the caller's first ratcheted frame, and on that side the CAPS handler runs in the task that reads the connection: the send waited on a read that task could no longer make. The caller was never answered and the handler never ended, even after the caller hung up, keeping one of that peer's inbound slots for the life of the daemon. The accepting side now hands the delivery to a tracked task, queued ahead of its own replies, and keeps reading. The calling side is unchanged.

After an independent review: with two or more certificates owed, only the first went out before the handler's first answer, because the delivery took the send lock once per certificate and the answer got in between. The accepting side's read loop now starts the delivery after CAPS and finishes it before it answers the next frame.

validation.summary: Three tests with the real handler, a real channel and a real state store. Against the code before the change, a caller that is owed a certificate gets no answer, the handler is still running after the caller has gone and one inbound slot stays held. After it the caller receives the certificate and then its answer, and nothing is left. The existing 114 rotation and capability tests pass.

It refuted the ordering for two or more certificates, 5 runs of 5, addressed as above; the test now owes one, two and three. Five planted defects are each caught. Read but not run by the reviewer: the calling side, the idle-timeout path, relay-backed channels.
